modules.title: Foundations: Products, Baking Science and Kitchen Safety
modules.overview: Before you weigh a single gram of flour, you need to know which products sell, why dough and batter behave the way they do, and how to keep food and people safe. This module gives you the map of the snacks business, the science of flour, yeast, fat, sugar and heat, and the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food applied to a small Nigerian kitchen.

lessons.title: The snacks business: five core products and where they sell
objectives: Name the five core products in this course and how each one is cooked
Group products by how quickly they spoil and what that means for selling
Identify at least three local outlets where baked goods and snacks sell
Choose a sensible first product for your budget, equipment and customers

blocks.text: Walk past any school gate, motor park, office building or church in Nigeria at break time and you will see the same snacks: **meat pie, chin chin, puff-puff, bread and cake**. They are popular because they are filling, affordable and familiar. This course teaches you to make all five properly, with weighed recipes, safe hygiene and honest costing, so that you can sell them with confidence or produce them for your family and events.

blocks.name: business-shop
blocks.alt: A woman standing at a small shop counter
blocks.caption: A small snacks business can start from a home kitchen and a table at the right spot.

blocks.text: Two families of products: baked and fried

Your five products fall into two groups. **Baked** products (bread, cake, meat pie) are cooked by hot, dry air in an oven. **Fried** products (chin chin, puff-puff) are cooked by hot oil in a pot or fryer. Fried snacks need only a gas or kerosene stove and a deep pot, so they are the cheapest way to start. Baked products need an oven, either a gas cooker oven, an electric oven or a locally made charcoal or gas baking oven, but they usually sell at a higher price per piece.

blocks.text: Why shelf life decides your selling plan

Shelf life is how long a product stays safe and pleasant to eat. A product with a **short shelf life**, like puff-puff or meat pie, must be made close to the time of sale. You cook in the morning and sell by afternoon, so you need a nearby, steady customer group: a school, an office, a market lane. A product with a **long shelf life**, like well-made chin chin, can be made once or twice a week, packed in sealed bags and sold slowly through shops and online orders. Many small producers combine both: chin chin as the steady earner, and puff-puff or meat pie as a daily fresh line.

items: Fresh line
Packed line
blocks.caption: Shelf life decides how often you produce and where you can sell.

blocks.text: Where baked goods and snacks sell

items: **Schools**: pupils and staff buy at break time; many schools also order for parties and end-of-term events.
**Offices and banks**: staff buy mid-morning; a weekly standing order is common once they trust you.
**Events**: birthdays, naming ceremonies, weddings and church programmes order small chops packs (puff-puff, meat pie, spring rolls, samosa) in bulk.
**Neighbourhood shops and supermarkets**: they stock sealed chin chin and cakes, usually on credit or sale-or-return terms.
**WhatsApp and Instagram**: customers order trays and packs for delivery; your status updates are your shop window.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a first product
blocks.context: For example, Bisi lives in Ibadan near a primary school with about 300 pupils. She has a two-burner gas stove, no oven, and about 25,000 naira (approximate) to start.
steps: Without an oven she sets aside bread, cake and meat pie for now.
She compares chin chin and puff-puff. Puff-puff must be sold hot and fresh, which suits the school break at 10:30 am.
She plans to fry one batch of puff-puff each school morning and sell at the gate, and to make chin chin on Saturdays for neighbours and a nearby shop.
She sets money aside to buy a small gas or charcoal oven later, once sales are steady, so she can add meat pie.
blocks.result: Bisi starts with two fried products that need only her stove, matches her fresh line to the school break, and has a clear next step towards baking.

blocks.title: How this course is built
blocks.text: Module 1 covers science and safety. Module 2 walks you through tested recipes with weights. Module 3 covers quality, labels and costing. Module 4 helps you plan production, sell, and finish your certificate project with real photos and records.

As you go, keep one notebook or one folder on your phone just for this course. Every recipe you try, every price you check and every photo you take becomes part of your final portfolio. Good bakers are not people who never fail. They are people who write down what they did, so they can repeat what worked and fix what did not.

Finally, think about your own time. Fried snacks are quick but you must stand at the stove. Bread needs waiting time for the dough to rise, which you can use for packing or cleaning. Meat pie takes the most hands-on work per piece. Choose a product that fits the hours you really have, not the hours you wish you had.

takeaways: The five core products are chin chin, puff-puff, meat pie, bread and cake
Fried snacks need only a stove; baked goods need an oven
Short shelf life means make close to sale; long shelf life means pack and sell slowly
Match each product to a real, nearby customer group before you start

lessons.title: Baking science: flour, gluten, leavening, fat, sugar and heat
objectives: Explain how gluten forms and why bread and pastry need different handling
Distinguish yeast, baking powder and baking soda and when each is used
Describe what fat, sugar and eggs do in a recipe
Choose the right oven or oil temperature for each core product

blocks.text: A recipe is not magic. Every ingredient has a job. When you understand those jobs, you can follow a recipe better, fix problems, and stop wasting flour. This lesson explains the five things that control almost every baked or fried snack: **flour and gluten, raising agents, fat, sugar, and heat**.

blocks.name: bread
blocks.caption: A soft loaf is the result of gluten, yeast gas and oven heat working together.

blocks.text: Flour and gluten

Wheat flour contains two proteins, **glutenin and gliadin**. When you add water and mix, they join to form **gluten**, a stretchy network. Kneading makes that network stronger and more elastic, like a net of rubber bands. In bread, this net traps the gas made by yeast so the dough rises and the loaf is chewy and light. In pastry and cake, you want the opposite: a short, tender bite, so you mix gently and briefly.

Flour with **more protein** forms stronger gluten. Bread flour is a higher-protein flour; cake and pastry flours are lower. Most Nigerian home bakers use one all-purpose wheat flour for everything and adjust the method: long kneading for bread, light rubbing and little water for pastry. Check the protein figure on your flour bag's nutrition panel if it is printed, and note it in your records.
Raising agents: what makes things rise

head: Raising agent
How it works
Used in
rows: A living fungus that eats sugar and gives off carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol. Needs warmth and time.
A ready mix of an alkali and an acid. Most is double acting: it releases some gas when wet and more when heated.
An alkali (sodium bicarbonate). Releases gas only when it meets an acid such as buttermilk, yoghurt or lemon juice.
Recipes that contain an acid ingredient
Air beaten into butter, sugar and eggs expands in the oven; water in dough turns to steam.

blocks.title: Yeast is alive
blocks.text: Use lukewarm water, comfortable on the inside of your wrist. Very hot water kills yeast and your dough will not rise. Keep salt from sitting directly on yeast for long, and store opened yeast sealed in a cool place.
Fat, sugar, eggs and salt

items: **Fat** (margarine, butter, oil) coats flour proteins and shortens gluten strands. That is why pastry with plenty of cold fat is crumbly and flaky. Fat also adds flavour and keeps bread and cake soft for longer.
**Sugar** sweetens, feeds yeast, helps crusts brown, and holds moisture so cakes stay soft. Too much sugar in fried dough makes it brown too fast on the outside before the inside cooks.
**Eggs** bind ingredients together, add richness, trap air when beaten, and set firm when heated, giving cake its structure.
**Salt** adds flavour and controls yeast so bread does not over-rise. Bread without salt tastes flat.

blocks.text: Heat: oven and oil temperatures

Heat sets the structure, cooks the starch and browns the surface. Too low and products are pale, greasy or doughy. Too high and they burn outside while staying raw inside. Use an **oven thermometer** if you can, because many home and local ovens run hotter or cooler than their dial says. For frying, a **deep-fry thermometer** removes guesswork. Without one, drop in a small piece of dough: it should sink slightly, then rise and bubble steadily within a few seconds.

blocks.title: What happens to bread in the oven
items: Gas expands, dough springs
Yeast dies, gluten sets
Starch cooks, crumb forms
Crust browns
blocks.caption: Each stage needs the right heat, which is why oven temperature matters.

head: Product
Typical temperature
Sign it is done
rows: Deep golden crust, sounds hollow when tapped underneath
Skewer in the centre comes out clean, top springs back
Pastry golden all over, base firm and not pale
Golden brown, cooked through, not greasy inside
Even golden colour, crunchy once cool

blocks.title: Worked example: diagnosing flat puff-puff
blocks.context: For example, Amaka's puff-puff batter did not rise after an hour, and the balls fried flat and heavy.
steps: She checks the yeast: the sachet was opened two months ago and left in a hot kitchen.
She checks the water: she used water just off the boil because the morning was cold.
Next batch she uses a fresh sachet of instant yeast and water that feels lukewarm on her wrist.
She covers the bowl and leaves it in a warm spot; in about 45 minutes it has doubled and is full of bubbles.
blocks.result: The cause was dead yeast from hot water and old stock. With live yeast and lukewarm water, the batter rose and the puff-puff came out light and round.

takeaways: Kneading builds gluten for chewy bread; gentle mixing keeps pastry and cake tender
Yeast needs warmth and time; baking powder works when wet and heated; baking soda needs an acid
Fat shortens gluten, sugar browns and softens, eggs bind and set
Correct oven and oil temperature is the difference between cooked and greasy or burnt
