lessons.title: Food hygiene with the WHO Five Keys, tools and kitchen safety
objectives: Apply the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food to a small baking kitchen
Keep perishable fillings out of the temperature danger zone
Set up a basic tool kit for weighed, repeatable baking
Prevent and respond to hot oil and gas cooking accidents

blocks.text: When you sell food, your customers trust you with their health. A single batch of meat pie with spoiled filling can make many people ill and end your business. The World Health Organization (WHO) sums up safe food handling in **Five Keys to Safer Food**. They are simple, and they apply directly to your kitchen.

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.alt: A person washing hands at a sink
blocks.caption: Clean hands and surfaces are the first of the WHO Five Keys.

blocks.title: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
items: Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
blocks.caption: These five habits prevent most foodborne illness in a small kitchen.

blocks.text: Key 1: Keep clean

Wash your hands with soap and clean water before handling food and often during work, especially after the toilet, after touching raw meat or eggs, after handling money and after touching your phone. Wash and sanitise surfaces and equipment. Keep insects, rodents and pets out of the work area. Tie back hair, cover it, remove rings and bracelets, and do not cook for sale when you have diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut.
Key 2: Separate raw and cooked

Raw minced meat for meat pie filling carries bacteria. Use a separate board and knife for raw meat, or wash them thoroughly with hot soapy water before using them for anything else. Never put cooked filling back into the bowl that held raw meat. Store raw meat below cooked or ready-to-eat food in the fridge so juices cannot drip onto it.
Key 3: Cook thoroughly

Cook minced meat until no pink remains and the juices run clear. WHO advises cooking food to at least **70 C** at the centre; a food thermometer lets you check. Cook the filling fully on the stove before it goes into the pastry, because the oven time for meat pie is mainly to cook the pastry, not the raw meat.
Key 4: Keep food at safe temperatures

Bacteria multiply fastest between **5 C and 60 C**, the temperature danger zone. Do not leave cooked filling or meat pies at room temperature for more than **2 hours**. If you cook filling the night before, cool it quickly in a shallow container and refrigerate it below 5 C. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not on the counter. Sell meat pies the same day, and do not keep unsold meat pies in a warm display case overnight.
Key 5: Use safe water and raw materials

Use treated or boiled water for dough and washing. Buy flour, margarine and eggs from sellers with good turnover, check dates and packaging, and reject flour with weevils, a musty smell or damp lumps. Do not use eggs with cracked shells. Frying oil that is dark, smoky, foamy or smells sharp has broken down and should be discarded.

Store dry ingredients off the floor, in sealed containers, away from damp walls and direct sun. Label each container with the date you opened it and use older stock first. Keep margarine and eggs cool. A tidy store protects your money as well as your customers.

blocks.title: Hot oil and gas
blocks.text: Never leave hot oil unattended and keep children away from the stove. Lower food into oil gently with a spoon, away from you. If oil catches fire, turn off the gas if you can reach it safely and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on an oil fire. Keep a fire extinguisher or fire blanket nearby, keep the gas cylinder upright and ventilated, and check hoses for leaks with soapy water, not a flame.

blocks.name: fire-extinguisher
blocks.caption: Keep a fire extinguisher or fire blanket within reach of your frying station.

blocks.text: Your starter tool kit

items: Digital kitchen scale reading in 1 g steps, the most important tool for repeatable results
Measuring spoons and a measuring jug
Large mixing bowls, a wooden spoon or spatula, a rolling pin and a sieve
Deep pot or fryer, slotted spoon, and a tray lined with paper to drain fried snacks
Baking trays, a cake tin, a loaf tin and a pie cutter or a round cutter
Oven thermometer and a food or deep-fry thermometer if you can afford them
Clean aprons, hair covers, and separate cloths for hands, surfaces and dishes

blocks.title: Worked example: a safe meat pie filling plan
blocks.context: For example, Fatima has an order of 60 meat pies for a Saturday naming ceremony at 11 am.
steps: Friday evening she cooks the minced beef filling until no pink remains, then spreads it in a shallow tray to cool quickly.
Within 2 hours of cooking she covers it and puts it in the fridge.
Saturday at 6 am she washes hands, sanitises the table, makes the pastry, and fills the pies with cold filling.
She bakes from 7 am, cools the pies on a rack, packs them in clean boxes at 9:30 am and delivers at 10:30 am.
blocks.result: The filling spent very little time in the danger zone, the pies reached the guests within about 3 hours of baking, and no raw meat touched cooked food.

takeaways: Follow the WHO Five Keys: keep clean, separate, cook thoroughly, safe temperatures, safe water and raw materials
Cook meat filling fully on the stove and keep it out of the 5 to 60 C danger zone
A digital scale is the most important baking tool
Never use water on an oil fire; turn off the gas and cover the pot

activity.title: Set up and audit your workstation
steps: Clear and clean one work area and list the tools you already have against the starter kit.
Put up a handwashing point with soap, clean water and a towel next to your work area.
Write the Five Keys on a card and stick it where you cook.
Check your gas hose with soapy water and note where your lid or fire blanket is kept.
activity.evidence: Two photos (clean workstation and handwashing point) and your tool checklist with gaps marked.

quiz.q: Bisi has a gas stove but no oven and wants to start selling next week. Which pair of products fits her setup best?
quiz.explain: Chin chin and puff-puff are fried, so they need only a stove and a deep pot. The others need an oven.

quiz.q: Why does bread dough need long kneading while pastry should be handled briefly?
options: Pastry has no flour in it
Kneading builds gluten, which bread needs for structure but makes pastry tough
quiz.explain: Gluten traps gas and gives bread its chew. In pastry, strong gluten makes it hard instead of short and flaky.

quiz.q: Amaka used water straight off the boil to start her puff-puff batter. What is the most likely result?
options: Batter does not rise because the yeast is killed
quiz.explain: Very hot water kills yeast. Use lukewarm water that feels comfortable on your wrist.

quiz.q: Fatima cooked meat pie filling at 8 pm. By when should it be in the fridge?
options: Never, filling is safe at room temperature
quiz.explain: Cooked food should not stay in the 5 to 60 C danger zone for more than 2 hours. Cool it in a shallow tray and refrigerate.

quiz.q: Oil in Kemi's frying pot catches fire. What should she do?
options: Pour a cup of water on it
Turn off the gas if safe and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket
Fan the flames to cool them
quiz.explain: Water makes burning oil explode outward. Cutting the heat and smothering the fire removes the oxygen.

quiz.q: Which raising agent needs an acid ingredient such as yoghurt or lemon juice to work?
quiz.explain: Baking soda is an alkali and only releases gas when it reacts with an acid. Baking powder already contains its own acid.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Tested Recipes from Chin Chin to Bread
modules.overview: This module puts the science to work with standard recipes written in grams. You will make chin chin and puff-puff, then meat pie and a simple pound cake, learn to scale a recipe for a big order, and finish with a basic white loaf and a simple tasting and feedback loop that improves every batch.

lessons.title: Weighing, mise en place and two fried snacks: chin chin and puff-puff
objectives: Follow a standard production workflow from weighing to packing
Make chin chin from a weighed recipe with an even, crunchy result
Make puff-puff with a properly risen batter and correct frying temperature
Cool and store fried snacks so they stay crisp and safe

blocks.text: Professional bakers weigh their ingredients. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 g to 160 g depending on how you scoop it, and that difference is enough to turn soft dough into hard dough. In this course every recipe is in **grams**, with spoons used only for small amounts such as salt, yeast and spices. Weigh everything, every time, and your chin chin will taste the same in the tenth batch as in the first.

blocks.name: doughnut
blocks.caption: Fried dough snacks like puff-puff depend on a well-risen batter and steady oil temperature.

blocks.text: The standard workflow

blocks.title: Production workflow
items: Clean and set up
Weigh all ingredients
Mix and rest
Shape and cook
Cool completely
Pack and label
blocks.caption: Use the same six stages for every product so nothing is forgotten.

blocks.text: Chefs call the second stage **mise en place**, French for 'everything in its place'. Before you mix, weigh every ingredient into its own bowl or cup and line them up. You will never discover halfway through that you have no eggs, and you will not forget the salt.
Recipe 1: Chin chin (500 g flour batch)

head: Ingredient
Amount
Job
rows: Milk (liquid, or powdered milk mixed with water)
Enough for 5 to 7 cm depth in the pot

items: Mix flour, sugar, nutmeg, salt and baking powder in a large bowl.
Rub the cold margarine into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs.
Beat the egg into the milk and add it a little at a time, mixing until you have a firm, smooth dough that does not stick to your hands. You may not need all the milk.
Cover and rest the dough for 10 minutes, then roll it out to about 5 mm thick.
Cut into small squares or strips about 1 cm wide. Keep pieces the same size so they cook evenly.
Heat oil to about 160 to 170 C. Fry in small batches, stirring often, until evenly golden.
Drain on a tray lined with paper and let it cool completely before packing in airtight bags or jars.

blocks.title: Why chin chin turns hard or soggy
blocks.text: Too much flour or too little fat gives rock-hard chin chin. Packing it while still warm traps steam and makes it soft and stale. Oil that is too hot browns the outside before the inside dries out, so it softens later.
Recipe 2: Puff-puff (500 g flour batch)

items: Mix flour, sugar, salt, nutmeg and yeast in a bowl.
Add lukewarm water gradually and beat by hand or with a wooden spoon for 3 to 5 minutes into a thick, smooth, stretchy batter, thicker than pancake batter.
Cover with a lid or cling film and leave in a warm place for 45 to 60 minutes, until doubled in size and full of bubbles.
Heat oil to about 170 to 180 C. Scoop batter with a wet hand or two spoons and drop small balls gently into the oil.
Turn them so they brown evenly. They are done when deep golden all over; break one open to check the centre is cooked.
Drain on paper. Serve the same day.

blocks.title: Worked example: weighing a double batch
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi has an order of about 80 puff-puff for a children's party and her single batch gives about 40 medium balls.
steps: She doubles every ingredient: 1,000 g flour, 200 g sugar, 14 g yeast (two sachets), 2 teaspoons salt, about 900 ml water.
She weighs each ingredient into its own bowl before she starts mixing.
She uses a larger bowl, because the batter will double in size.
She fries in batches of about 10 so the oil temperature does not drop.
blocks.result: The double batch rises evenly and gives about 80 balls of similar size. Frying small batches keeps them golden instead of pale and oily.

blocks.text: When frying any snack, do not crowd the pot. Each piece of cold dough cools the oil. Too many pieces at once drop the temperature, and the snack soaks up oil instead of sealing quickly. A thermometer, or the test of a small piece that rises and bubbles within a few seconds, keeps you on track.

takeaways: Weigh every ingredient in grams; cups are too inconsistent
Set out all ingredients before mixing (mise en place)
Chin chin: firm dough, even pieces, oil about 160 to 170 C, cool fully before packing
Puff-puff: live yeast, doubled bubbly batter, oil about 170 to 180 C, small batches

activity.title: Fry and record one batch
steps: Choose chin chin or puff-puff and weigh every ingredient for one batch.
Photograph your mise en place before mixing.
Make the batch, noting oil temperature or your test-piece result, and frying time per batch.
Count or weigh the finished yield and note any pieces that were pale, burnt or greasy.
activity.evidence: Photos of mise en place and finished product, plus a note of weights, yield and problems.

lessons.title: Meat pie and pound cake, and scaling a recipe for a big order
objectives: Make shortcrust pastry and a fully cooked meat pie filling
Shape, egg-wash and bake meat pies to an even golden finish
Make a pound cake using the creaming method
Scale any recipe up or down using a multiplication factor

blocks.text: Meat pie is the queen of Nigerian small chops: a short, buttery pastry around a savoury filling of minced meat, potato and carrot. It is more work than fried snacks, but it sells at a higher price and is always in demand for events. This lesson gives you a standard recipe, a pound cake as your second oven product, and the method to scale both for big orders.

blocks.name: pie
blocks.caption: Good meat pie pastry is short, flaky and golden on the top and the base.

blocks.text: Meat pie pastry (makes about 12 pies)

The **baker's percentage** column shows each ingredient as a share of the flour weight, with flour always 100%. Here the fat is half the flour weight. This makes scaling easy: if you use 1,000 g of flour, you need 500 g of fat.
Filling

items: 300 g minced beef
250 g Irish potatoes, peeled and cut into small cubes
100 g carrots, cut into small cubes
1 medium onion, chopped
1 teaspoon curry powder, 1 teaspoon dried thyme, 1 seasoning cube, salt to taste
2 tablespoons flour mixed into about 150 ml cold water to thicken
Filling: cook the beef and onion in a pot, stirring, until no pink remains. Add curry, thyme, seasoning and a little water. Add potatoes and carrots and cook until just tender.
Stir in the flour and water mix and cook for a few minutes until thick, so the filling is moist but not runny. Taste for salt. Spread on a tray to cool, and refrigerate if not using within 2 hours.
Pastry: mix flour, baking powder and salt. Rub in the cold margarine until it looks like breadcrumbs. Add cold water a little at a time and bring together into a soft dough. Do not knead.
Wrap and chill the dough for about 20 minutes so the fat firms up.
Roll to about 3 to 4 mm thick and cut circles about 12 to 15 cm across with a cutter or saucer.
Put a spoonful of cold filling on one half, brush the edge with water, fold over and press shut with a fork.
Place on a greased or lined tray, brush with beaten egg, and bake at about 180 to 200 C for 25 to 35 minutes, until golden on top and firm underneath.

blocks.title: Never fill pastry with hot or raw filling
blocks.text: Hot filling melts the fat in the pastry and makes the base soggy. Raw meat may not reach a safe temperature in the oven. Always cook the filling fully, then cool it before filling.

items: **Keep it cold**: cold fat makes flaky layers. On hot days, chill the flour and work early in the morning.
**Do not overwork**: stop mixing as soon as the dough holds together, or gluten develops and the pastry turns hard.
**Roll evenly**: thin spots burn and leak; thick spots stay raw.
**Seal well**: press the edges firmly with a fork so the filling does not burst out.
**Bake fully**: lift one pie and check that the base is golden, not pale and soft.

blocks.text: Pound cake (one 20 cm round tin)

A classic pound cake uses **equal weights** of fat, sugar, eggs and flour, which makes it easy to remember: 250 g margarine or butter, 250 g sugar, 250 g eggs (about 5 medium eggs out of the shell), 250 g flour, plus 1 teaspoon baking powder, 1 teaspoon vanilla and a pinch of salt. Cream the soft fat and sugar for 5 to 8 minutes until pale and fluffy, beat in the eggs one at a time, then gently fold in the flour and baking powder. Bake in a greased and lined tin at about 170 C for 45 to 60 minutes, until a skewer in the centre comes out clean. Do not open the oven door in the first half of baking, or the cake may sink.
Scaling a recipe

blocks.title: How to scale any recipe
items: Target yield
Divide by recipe yield
Get the factor
Multiply every ingredient
Round and record
blocks.caption: One factor, applied to every ingredient, keeps the recipe balanced.

blocks.title: Worked example: 60 meat pies for an event
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna gets an order for 60 meat pies. Her recipe makes 12.
steps: Factor = 60 / 12 = 5.
Pastry: flour 500 g x 5 = 2,500 g; margarine 250 g x 5 = 1,250 g; water about 120 ml x 5 = 600 ml; baking powder 5 teaspoons; salt 2.5 teaspoons.
Filling: beef 300 g x 5 = 1,500 g; potatoes 1,250 g; carrots 500 g; 5 onions; 10 tablespoons flour in about 750 ml water.
She adds about 10% extra pastry and filling (about 6 pies) to cover breakages and a tasting sample.
She mixes the pastry in two or three smaller batches, because a huge batch is hard to rub in evenly and warms up.
blocks.result: Hauwa produces 66 pies, delivers 60, keeps a few for quality checks, and records the scaled recipe for future orders.

blocks.text: When you make many times a recipe, it is safer to mix in several normal-sized batches rather than one giant one. Ovens also hold only so many trays, so plan your baking in rounds and keep unbaked pies cool while they wait their turn.

takeaways: Meat pie pastry is about half as much cold fat as flour; rub in, do not knead
Cook the filling fully, thicken it, and cool it before filling
Pound cake uses equal weights of fat, sugar, eggs and flour, creamed well
Scale with one factor (target yield divided by recipe yield) and add a small extra margin

activity.title: Bake and scale
steps: Make one batch of meat pies or one pound cake following the recipe in grams.
Photograph the product before baking and after baking, including the underside of one pie or the cut cake.
Write the scaled recipe for 50 pieces (or for three cakes), showing your factor and every new weight.
Note one thing you would change next time and why.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos plus a written scaled recipe showing the factor and new weights.

lessons.title: A basic white loaf, tasting panel and the feedback loop
objectives: Make a basic white loaf, including kneading, two rises and baking
Use the windowpane test and doneness checks with confidence
Run a simple tasting panel with a score sheet
Change one variable at a time to improve a product

blocks.text: Bread is the best teacher in baking because every step shows in the final loaf. If you rush the kneading or the rise, the crumb is dense. If you get it right, you have a soft, tall loaf that slices cleanly. In this lesson you will bake one loaf, then use a tasting panel to improve it, the same loop you will use for every product you sell.

blocks.name: baguette-bread
blocks.caption: Kneading, rising and baking time all show in the crust and crumb of a loaf.

blocks.text: Basic white loaf (one loaf tin)

items: Mix flour, sugar, yeast and salt. Add lukewarm water and bring together into a rough dough.
Knead on a clean table for 10 to 15 minutes. Add the soft margarine after the first few minutes and knead until the dough is smooth and springy.
Do the **windowpane test**: stretch a small piece thin between your fingers. If it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, the gluten is ready.
Put the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.
Press out the air, shape into a tight log, and place in a greased loaf tin, seam down.
Cover and let it rise again for 30 to 45 minutes, until it rises just above the rim of the tin.
Bake at about 200 C for 25 to 30 minutes until deep golden. Tip it out and tap the bottom: it should sound hollow. If you have a probe thermometer, the centre should reach about 90 C or more.
Cool on a rack for at least an hour before slicing, or the inside will be gummy.

blocks.title: Rising times are a guide
blocks.text: Yeast works faster in a hot kitchen and slower on harmattan mornings or in air conditioning. Judge the dough by size and feel, not only by the clock. A gentle finger press that springs back slowly means it is ready.

Many loaves sold in Nigeria are softer and sweeter than this basic one because they contain more sugar and fat. Once your basic loaf works, you can raise sugar towards 10 to 12% and fat towards 8 to 10% of the flour weight, one step at a time, and record how the softness and colour change. More sugar browns faster, so watch the crust.
The feedback loop

blocks.title: Improve one batch at a time
items: Bake and record
Taste and score
Find the weakest point
Change one thing
Bake again
blocks.caption: Changing only one thing per batch shows you exactly what made the difference.

blocks.text: Ask three to five people who will be honest, ideally people who are like your future customers, to taste your product. Give each person a simple **score sheet** with scores from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) for appearance, texture, taste and size for the price. Add one open question: 'What one thing would make you buy this again?' Do not tell them what you think of it first, or they will agree with you.

head: Criterion
What to look for
Score 1 to 5
rows: Even golden colour, good shape, no burnt spots
Bread soft and springy; chin chin crunchy; pie pastry flaky
Balanced salt and sugar, no raw flour or oily taste
Size feels fair for the planned price

blocks.text: Record every bake on one line or one page: date, flour brand, water temperature (or 'lukewarm'), kneading time, first and second rise times, oven setting, baking time, loaf weight and the average panel scores. These notes let you see patterns, such as slower rises on cold mornings, that you would otherwise forget.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a dense loaf
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt baked her first loaf. Her four tasters scored texture an average of 2 out of 5 and said it was heavy and tight.
steps: She checks her notes: she kneaded for only 5 minutes and the first rise took 40 minutes in an air-conditioned room.
She decides to change one thing only: kneading time, increased to 12 minutes, with a windowpane test.
Second loaf: the texture average rises to 3.5. Tasters now say it is soft but a little pale.
For the third loaf she keeps 12 minutes of kneading and bakes 5 minutes longer. The appearance score rises from 3 to 4.
blocks.result: By changing one variable per bake, Grace learned that kneading fixed the density and longer baking fixed the colour. She writes both into her standard recipe.

blocks.text: Keep every score sheet. Over a few batches you will see your scores climb, and these sheets become strong evidence for your certificate portfolio and for customers who ask why they should trust you.

takeaways: A basic loaf is 100% flour, about 60% water, with small amounts of yeast, salt, sugar and fat
The windowpane test shows when gluten is developed
Judge rising by size and feel; bake until hollow-sounding and golden
Score with a small honest panel and change only one variable per batch

activity.title: Bake, score and improve
steps: Bake one loaf (or a batch of any product from this module) and note every time and temperature.
Ask at least three people to score it on the four criteria with the score sheet.
Identify the lowest-scoring criterion and choose one change to fix it.
Bake a second batch with only that change and score it again.
activity.evidence: Photos of both batches (including a cut slice), both sets of score sheets, and a short note on what changed.

quiz.q: Why does this course give flour in grams instead of cups?
options: A cup of flour can vary a lot in weight, so grams give repeatable results
Cups are not sold in Nigeria
Grams make the dough rise faster
quiz.explain: How you scoop changes how much flour fits in a cup. Weighing removes that variation.

quiz.q: Ada packed her chin chin in sealed bags while it was still warm. Two days later it is soft. What went wrong?
options: Trapped steam from the warm chin chin softened it
Chin chin always goes soft in two days
quiz.explain: Warm snacks release steam. Sealing them before they cool traps moisture and ruins the crunch.

quiz.q: Hauwa's meat pie recipe makes 12 pies and needs 250 g margarine. How much margarine does she need for 48 pies?
Why should meat pie filling be cooled before it goes into the pastry?
options: Hot filling melts the fat and makes the base soggy
quiz.explain: Pastry relies on firm fat for flakiness. Hot filling melts it and the base becomes soggy and pale.

quiz.q: Grace's loaf was dense and her tasters scored the colour low too. What is the best next step?
options: Change the flour, yeast and oven temperature all at once
Change only one thing, such as kneading time, and test again
quiz.explain: Changing one variable per batch shows which change fixed which problem.

quiz.q: In the pound cake method, what is the purpose of creaming fat and sugar for 5 to 8 minutes?
options: To beat in air that helps the cake rise and stay light
quiz.explain: Creaming traps tiny air bubbles that expand in the oven, working alongside the baking powder.

modules.title: Quality, Labelling and Costing
modules.overview: Customers come back for products that are the same good quality every time, honestly labelled and fairly priced. This module teaches you to inspect and fix common faults, declare allergens and write a correct label, understand the basics of NAFDAC registration for packaged food, and keep batch records that show your true cost and profit per piece.

lessons.title: Quality standards and fixing common baking and frying faults
objectives: Describe the quality standard for each of the five core products
Diagnose common faults from what you see, feel and taste
Choose the correct fix for each fault
Run a quick quality check before any batch leaves your kitchen

blocks.text: A **quality standard** is a short description of what a good product looks, feels and tastes like, written down so that you, or anyone helping you, can check every batch against it. Without a standard, quality drifts: one day the chin chin is crunchy and golden, the next it is pale and hard, and customers notice before you do.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: A written quality checklist makes every batch consistent, even when someone else helps.

blocks.text: What good looks like

head: Product
Look
Texture and taste
rows: Even golden brown, pieces the same size
Crunchy, not rock hard, lightly sweet, no oily or burnt taste
Round, deep golden, no pale patches
Light and airy inside, fully cooked, not soaked in oil
Golden top and base, edges sealed, no leaks
Short, flaky pastry; moist, well-seasoned filling
Tall, even golden crust, good shape
Soft, springy crumb with small even holes, not gummy
Flat or gently domed top, even colour
Moist, fine crumb, no sunken centre or raw streak

blocks.text: Common faults and their fixes

head: Fault
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Heat oil to the right temperature, fry fewer pieces at a time
Oil or oven too hot, pieces too big
Lower the heat, make pieces smaller and even
Dead yeast, too little rising time, batter too thin
Fresh yeast, lukewarm water, let it double, adjust water
Too much flour or too little fat, overworked dough
Weigh accurately, rub in fat well, handle dough lightly
Hot filling, runny filling, oven too cool
Cool and thicken filling, bake hotter or on a lower shelf
Overmixed, too much water, warm fat
Mix briefly, add water slowly, keep fat cold
Knead to windowpane, let dough double
Oven door opened early, too much raising agent, underbaked
Keep the door shut, measure baking powder exactly, test with a skewer

blocks.title: Change one thing at a time
blocks.text: When you fix a fault, change only one cause per batch and write it down. If you change three things at once and the product improves, you will not know which change worked.
Consistency: same size, same weight

Customers judge value by size. If one meat pie is big and the next is small, they feel cheated. Weigh your dough pieces and fillings. For example, cut meat pie circles with the same cutter and use the same spoon of filling. For puff-puff, aim for balls of the same size by using the same scoop. For chin chin, weigh each pack on your scale before sealing, and never sell packs below the weight printed on the label.

blocks.title: Pre-release quality check
items: Colour even and correct
Fully cooked inside
Size and weight consistent
Taste test passed
Cooled before packing
blocks.caption: Run these five checks on a sample from every batch before it leaves your kitchen.

blocks.title: Worked example: a batch that fails the check
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin fries 3 kg of chin chin for a supermarket order. During her check she finds about one in five pieces pale and soft inside.
steps: She breaks open five pale pieces: the centres are still slightly doughy.
She checks her notes: she fried larger batches than usual to save time, so the oil temperature dropped.
She sorts the batch, keeping only fully golden pieces for the supermarket, and uses the pale pieces for family.
For the next order, she fries in smaller batches and waits for the oil to recover between batches.
blocks.result: Rukayat delivers a smaller but fully good order and explains the short delivery to the shop owner, who appreciates the honesty. The fix becomes part of her standard method.

blocks.text: Keep one sample of each batch for a few days, sealed and labelled with the batch date. If a customer complains, you can taste the same batch and see whether the problem is real. Over time, these samples also tell you how long each product truly stays good, which you need for honest labelling in the next lesson.

Finally, look at your oven. Many ovens heat unevenly, with one corner hotter than the others. Turn trays halfway through baking, and note which shelf position gives the best results. This simple habit removes many 'mystery' faults.

Treat every customer comment as quality data. When someone says the puff-puff was oily or the meat pie was small, write it down with the date and batch number, thank them, and check the batch sample. If two or three people mention the same thing, it is a real pattern and goes to the top of your list of things to fix. Complaints handled politely often turn into your most loyal customers.

takeaways: Write a short quality standard for each product and check every batch against it
Most fried-snack faults come from wrong oil temperature or overcrowding
Most pastry and bread faults come from temperature of fat, mixing time and rising time
Weigh portions for consistent size, and keep a sample from each batch

activity.title: Write your quality standard
steps: Choose two products you have made in this course.
Write a three-line quality standard for each: look, texture, taste.
Make one batch and run the five-point pre-release check on a sample.
If any check fails, name the likely cause and the fix you will try.
activity.evidence: Your written quality standards, a completed check for one batch, and a photo of a cut or broken sample.

lessons.title: Allergens, honest labels, shelf life and NAFDAC basics
objectives: Identify common allergens in your products and declare them clearly
Write a label that includes the main elements required for pre-packaged food in Nigeria
Set a realistic shelf life from your own storage tests
Outline the steps towards NAFDAC registration for a packaged product

blocks.text: Selling food is a promise. Your label tells the customer what is inside, how much there is, who made it and until when it is good. An honest label protects people with food allergies, builds trust with shops, and is required for packaged food sold in Nigeria. This lesson covers allergens, label contents, shelf life and the first steps towards NAFDAC registration.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: A clear label tells customers what is inside, who made it, and when it should be eaten by.

blocks.text: Allergens in your products

An **allergen** is an ingredient that can cause a serious reaction in some people. Reactions range from a rash to difficulty breathing. You cannot see which customer is allergic, so you must declare allergens on the label and be ready to answer questions honestly.

head: Allergen
Where it appears in this course
rows: All five products: flour is the main ingredient
Chin chin, meat pie pastry egg wash, cake
Chin chin (milk), butter, some margarines and cake recipes
Some margarines and vegetable oils; check the label of what you buy
Only if you add them, or use groundnut oil; also a risk if you share equipment with nut snacks

blocks.title: Do not claim what you cannot prove
blocks.text: Never write 'gluten-free', 'sugar-free', 'cures' or 'healthy for diabetics' on your snacks. These are claims you cannot support, and nutritional claims on packaged food must be backed by evidence. If you use the same oil to fry groundnuts, say so, because traces can transfer.
What goes on a pre-packaged food label
Nigeria's NAFDAC Pre-packaged Food (Labelling) Regulations 2022 set out what a label must show. The main elements are:

items: The **name of the food**, describing what it really is, for example 'Chin Chin (fried sweet wheat snack)'
**Ingredients in descending order of weight**, with allergens clearly indicated
**Net content** in metric units, grams for solids
**Date of manufacture and expiry date**, written in full with day, month and year
**Name and address** of the manufacturer
A **batch number** so each production run can be traced
All information in **English**, with no false or misleading words or pictures
Once registered, the product's **NAFDAC registration number**

blocks.title: Worked example: a chin chin label
blocks.context: For example, Uche in Enugu packs chin chin in 150 g pouches for two neighbourhood shops.
steps: Name: Mama Uche's Chin Chin, fried sweet wheat snack.
Ingredients: wheat flour, sugar, margarine (vegetable oils, water, salt, milk solids), vegetable oil, egg, milk, nutmeg, baking powder, salt. Allergens: wheat (gluten), egg, milk; may contain soy.
Net weight: 150 g. Made: 03 October 2026. Expiry: 03 November 2026. Batch: CC-261003.
Made by: her registered business name and full address, plus a phone number for complaints.
blocks.result: The label lists everything a customer needs. Uche bases the expiry date on her own storage test, not on a guess, and records batch CC-261003 in her production book.

blocks.text: Setting shelf life honestly

Shelf life depends on moisture, fat, packaging and storage. Dry, well-sealed chin chin keeps much longer than bread or cake, but the fat in it slowly goes **rancid**, giving a stale, paint-like smell. Test your own: keep sealed packs from one batch at room temperature, open one each week, and note when the taste, smell or crunch changes. Set your expiry date safely before that point. Fresh products like meat pie and puff-puff should be sold and eaten the same day.

Packaging matters for shelf life and safety too. Use clean, food-grade pouches, jars or boxes, never reused cement, chemical or fertiliser bags. Heat-sealed pouches keep moisture out of chin chin far better than knotted nylon. Add a short storage line to the label, such as 'Store in a cool, dry place. Reseal after opening.' Keep packed stock off the floor and away from sunlight, which speeds up rancidity.
NAFDAC registration: the basic path

blocks.title: Path to a NAFDAC number
items: Register business with CAC
Prepare clean premises
Apply to NAFDAC
Inspection and sample tests
Receive registration number
blocks.caption: Packaged food for shops and supermarkets needs NAFDAC registration; plan for each step.

blocks.text: Pre-packaged food made in Nigeria for sale through shops and supermarkets must be registered with **NAFDAC** (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control). The usual path is: register your business name with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**, prepare hygienic production premises, apply to NAFDAC, allow inspection of your premises and testing of product samples, then receive a registration number to print on your label. NAFDAC has a desk for **micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs)**. Fees, documents and timelines change, so check the current requirements directly with NAFDAC's website or your nearest state office before you spend money on printed labels.

blocks.title: Never use potassium bromate
blocks.text: Potassium bromate is a banned bread improver in Nigeria. If anyone sells you a 'bread improver', read its ingredients and refuse any product that contains it.

takeaways: Wheat, eggs and milk are in most of your products; declare them on every label
Labels need name, ingredients by weight, net content, full dates, maker's name and address, batch number, in English
Set expiry dates from your own storage test, not a guess
Shop and supermarket products need NAFDAC registration; check current requirements with NAFDAC directly

activity.title: Draft your label and start a shelf-life test
steps: Choose one packaged product (for example chin chin) and list every ingredient by weight, heaviest first.
Mark the allergens and draft a full label with all the required elements.
Seal four packs from one batch, label them with the date, and store them at room temperature.
Open one pack each week and note smell, taste and crunch.
activity.evidence: A photo or file of your draft label and your shelf-life test notes with dates.

lessons.title: Batch records, cost per piece and simple business numbers
objectives: Keep a batch record that links ingredients, yield and quality
Calculate the full cost of a batch and the cost per piece or pack
Set a selling price that covers costs and gives a profit
Track four simple numbers that show whether your business is working

blocks.text: Many small food sellers work hard every day and still have no money at the end of the month. The usual reason is not laziness but **unknown costs**: gas, oil, packaging and broken pieces are forgotten, so the selling price is too low. In this lesson you will cost a batch properly and track a few numbers each week.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person using a large calculator
blocks.caption: A simple costing sheet shows the real cost of every pack you sell.

blocks.text: The batch record

A **batch record** is one page or one line in a notebook or spreadsheet for every batch. It should show: batch number, date, product, the weight of each ingredient, oil and oven temperatures, cooking time, yield (number of pieces or packs), rejects, and quality check result. You already used parts of this in Module 2. Now add the money.
Full cost of a batch

blocks.title: What your price must cover
items: Profit
Your labour
Gas, power, transport
Packaging and labels
Ingredients
blocks.caption: Build the price from the bottom up; profit only starts after every cost is covered.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing one chin chin batch
blocks.context: For example, Uche costs one 500 g flour batch of chin chin. The prices below are example prices only (approximate, in naira); check your own market, because prices change often.
steps: Ingredients: flour 500 g about 900; sugar 100 g about 250; margarine 100 g about 500; 1 egg about 250; milk about 300; nutmeg, baking powder and salt about 100; share of frying oil about 800. Total ingredients: about 3,100 naira.
Gas share for mixing and frying: about 400 naira.
Packaging: 10 pouches about 1,000 and 10 printed labels about 500. Total packaging: about 1,500 naira.
Full batch cost: 3,100 + 400 + 1,500 = about 5,000 naira.
Yield: about 700 g of chin chin, packed as ten 70 g pouches. Cost per pouch: 5,000 / 10 = about 500 naira.
She also wants to pay herself for 2 hours of work, about 1,000 naira per batch, or 100 naira per pouch. True cost per pouch: about 600 naira.
blocks.result: If Uche sells at 900 naira per pouch, she makes about 300 naira profit per pouch after paying herself. If she sold at 600 naira, she would only be paying herself, with nothing left to grow the business.

blocks.text: Setting the selling price

A simple method is **cost-plus**: true cost per piece plus a profit margin. Then check it against the market. If similar chin chin in your area sells at 800 to 1,000 naira for a similar size (example figures), and your true cost is 600, a price of 900 works. If the market price is below your cost, you must reduce costs (buy flour by the bag, buy packaging in bulk, cut waste), make a better product people will pay more for, or choose a different product.

head: Term
Meaning
Example from above
rows: Full batch cost divided by good units
Selling price minus cost per unit
Profit as a share of selling price

blocks.title: Wholesale price
blocks.text: Shops need their own profit, so they buy at a lower price than you sell to customers directly. Work out your wholesale price from your true cost first, so you never agree to a shop price that is below your cost.
Cutting costs without cutting quality

items: Buy flour, sugar and oil in larger quantities once you know your weekly usage, and store them properly so nothing spoils.
Buy packaging and labels in bulk; printing 500 labels usually costs far less per label than printing 20.
Reduce waste: weigh portions, fry in correct batches, and plan production to match orders.
Strain and reuse frying oil only while it is still clean and light; discard it once it darkens, smokes or foams.
Group baking so the oven is full each time it is heated, saving gas.

blocks.text: Four numbers to track every week

items: **Units sold** of each product
**Waste**: units unsold, burnt or rejected, as a share of units made
**Profit**: total sales minus total costs for the week
**Repeat customers**: how many people bought again

blocks.text: Write these four numbers in a simple weekly table, on paper or in a free spreadsheet app on your phone. After a month you will see which product makes the most profit, which day sells best, and where waste eats your money. Keep business money separate from household money, even if it is only a separate envelope or a separate account on Opay, Moniepoint or your bank app.

Review your costing sheet every month, or sooner when flour or oil prices jump. A price that was profitable three months ago may now be a loss. When you must raise prices, tell regular customers early and explain simply, for example that flour has gone up, rather than quietly shrinking the size.

takeaways: Keep a batch record that includes weights, yield, rejects and quality result
Full cost includes ingredients, oil, gas, packaging, labels and your own labour
Cost per unit equals full batch cost divided by good units
Track units sold, waste, profit and repeat customers every week

activity.title: Cost one real batch
steps: Choose one product and write the current price you pay for each ingredient and packaging item.
Calculate the full batch cost, including gas and your labour.
Divide by your actual good yield to get cost per unit.
Set a retail price and a wholesale price, and compare them with two local competitors.
activity.evidence: A completed costing sheet (photo or spreadsheet screenshot) with cost per unit, both prices and competitor prices.

quiz.q: Rukayat's puff-puff come out greasy and pale. What is the most likely cause?
options: Oil too cool or too many pieces in the pot
quiz.explain: Cool oil, often caused by overcrowding, lets the dough soak up oil before it seals and browns.

quiz.q: Which of these must appear on a pre-packaged chin chin label in Nigeria?
options: Ingredients in descending order of weight, with allergens indicated
The selling price at every shop
quiz.explain: The labelling regulations require ingredients by weight with allergens clearly indicated, plus name, net content, dates, maker and batch number.

quiz.q: Uche's chin chin batch costs 5,000 naira and gives 10 good pouches. If she adds 1,000 naira for her labour, what is her true cost per pouch?
A meat pie customer asks whether your pies contain egg. The pastry has no egg but you brush the tops with egg wash. What should you say?
options: Yes, the tops are brushed with egg
Only a little, so it does not count
quiz.explain: Egg wash is still egg. Allergen answers must be complete and honest.

quiz.q: How should Uche decide the expiry date for her chin chin?
options: Copy the date on a big brand's pack
Test sealed packs from her own batch over time and set the date before quality drops
quiz.explain: Shelf life depends on her own recipe, packaging and storage, so it must come from her own test.

quiz.q: A shop offers to buy Uche's pouches at 550 naira each. Her true cost is 600 naira. What should she do?
options: Accept, because volume is always good
Decline or negotiate, because she would lose 50 naira on every pouch
Accept and reduce the pouch weight without telling anyone
quiz.explain: A wholesale price below true cost means a loss on every unit. Reducing weight secretly would also be dishonest.

modules.title: Production, Selling and Your Certificate Project
modules.overview: In this final module you bring everything together. You will plan a real production day for an order, assemble your portfolio, package and price your products, sell through WhatsApp, schools, offices and shops while staying safe from payment scams, and finish with your certification checklist and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Planning a production day and building your project portfolio
objectives: Work backwards from a delivery time to plan a production day
Prepare a shopping list and equipment plan from a scaled recipe
Run a full order from shopping to delivery with records
Assemble a portfolio that proves your practical competence

blocks.text: Your final project is a real order, or a realistic practice order, produced from start to finish with records and photos. The secret of a calm production day is planning backwards from the delivery time. Professional caterers do this for every event, and it is the difference between a smooth morning and burnt pies at 10 am.

blocks.name: schedule
blocks.alt: A person arranging tasks on a large calendar
blocks.caption: Planning backwards from the delivery time keeps a production day calm and on schedule.

blocks.text: Plan backwards from delivery

items: Write the delivery time and place, and how long the journey takes.
Allow time for packing and cooling: baked and fried goods must cool before closing boxes or bags.
Count oven rounds or frying batches, and how long each takes.
Add preparation time: weighing, mixing, rising, filling, shaping.
Put shopping and anything you can do safely the day before (dry weighing, cooking and chilling filling) on the previous day.

blocks.title: Production day for 50 meat pies and 100 puff-puff
items: Day before: shop, cook filling
5:30 am: pastry and batter
6:30 am: bake pies in rounds
8:30 am: fry puff-puff
9:30 am: cool, pack, label
10:30 am: deliver
blocks.caption: Every step is placed by working backwards from the 10:30 am delivery.

blocks.title: Worked example: a mixed small chops order
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Abuja receives an order for 50 meat pies and 100 puff-puff to be delivered at 10:30 am on Saturday, 30 minutes from her home. Her oven bakes 16 pies per round in about 30 minutes.
steps: She scales her recipes: meat pie factor 50 / 12, about 4.2, so she makes 5 batches of pastry and filling to allow a margin; puff-puff factor 100 / 40 = 2.5, so 3 batches of batter.
She needs 4 oven rounds for 55 pies: about 2 hours including loading. She starts baking at 6:30 am, so pastry must be made and chilled by 6:15 am.
Puff-puff batter needs about 1 hour to rise, so she mixes it at 7:30 am and fries from 8:30 am while the last pies cool.
Friday: she shops, checks her gas level, cooks the filling, cools and refrigerates it within 2 hours, and weighs all dry ingredients into labelled bags.
She packs at 9:30 am and leaves at 10:00 am.
blocks.result: Halima delivers on time with 5 spare pies for quality checks. Her plan, batch records and photos go straight into her portfolio.

blocks.title: Have a plan B
blocks.text: Check your gas the day before and know where to refill early in the morning. If power or gas fails, a neighbour's oven or an extra gas cylinder can save the order. Tell the customer early if anything will be late.
Production day checklist

items: Gas cylinder level checked, and a spare or refill plan ready
Oven and stove tested; oven thermometer in place
All ingredients bought, checked for freshness and weighed
Clean trays, bowls, cutters, slotted spoons and cooling racks ready
Enough boxes, pouches, labels and paper liners for the full order plus a few extra
Handwashing point, aprons, hair covers and clean cloths set out

blocks.text: Start the day by cleaning and sanitising your work surfaces, even if you cleaned the night before. Tie and cover your hair, wash your hands, and keep raw meat work separate from finished products. Keep children and visitors out of the kitchen while oil is hot and the oven is on.

Delivery is part of production. Pack boxes flat and upright in a clean carton or cool box, keep them out of direct sun, and do not leave meat pies in a hot car. Bring a copy of the order and get the customer to confirm receipt, either by signature or a WhatsApp message.
Your project portfolio

Your portfolio is the proof that you can produce safe, consistent, profitable products, not only that you read the lessons. Keep it in one folder on your phone or in a printed file. It should contain:

items: Your standard recipes in grams for at least two products, one fried and one baked if you have an oven
Photos: clean workstation, mise en place, products during cooking, finished products, a cut or broken sample
Batch records with weights, temperatures, yields and quality check results
A costing sheet with cost per unit, retail price and wholesale price
A draft label for any packed product, with allergens
Tasting panel score sheets from at least three people, and a short note on what you changed
Your production plan for one real or practice order

blocks.text: Quality matters more than quantity. Five clear, honest photos with dates are better than thirty blurry ones. Take photos in daylight near a window, on a clean plain surface, and show the product close up. These same photos will later become your WhatsApp catalogue.

takeaways: Plan every order backwards from the delivery time
Do safe preparation the day before, such as cooking and chilling filling
Allow time for cooling and packing, and keep a small margin of extra pieces
Your portfolio proves real practice: recipes, photos, records, costing, label and feedback

activity.title: Plan and run one order
steps: Take a real order or set a practice order of at least 30 pieces.
Write a backwards plan with times, a shopping list and scaled recipes.
Produce the order, keeping a batch record and taking photos at each stage.
Write three lines on what went well and what you would change.
activity.evidence: Your written production plan, batch record, stage photos and three-line review.

lessons.title: Packaging, pricing and selling to customers, schools and shops
objectives: Choose packaging that protects the product and looks professional
Present clear retail and wholesale prices
Sell through WhatsApp Business, institutions and shops
Receive payments safely and avoid common payment scams

blocks.text: A good product still needs to reach buyers. In this lesson you will package it well, present prices clearly, find customers in three main channels, and protect your money when people pay by transfer.

blocks.name: messaging
blocks.alt: A person sending messages on a phone
blocks.caption: WhatsApp is often the main shop window for small food businesses in Nigeria.

blocks.text: Packaging that sells

items: **Chin chin**: clear heat-sealed pouches or plastic jars, so customers see the colour; label on the front.
**Meat pie and puff-puff**: clean food boxes or trays with a lid, lined with food-grade paper to absorb oil.
**Bread**: food-grade bread bags, closed only after the loaf has fully cooled.
**Cake**: cake boxes or sealed slices in clear wrap, labelled with date and allergens.
Use food-grade materials only, and keep the packaging store clean and dry.

blocks.text: Retail and wholesale prices

blocks.title: Retail vs wholesale
items: Retail (direct to customer)
Wholesale (to shops)
blocks.caption: Both channels can work, as long as each price is above your true cost.

blocks.text: Make a one-page price list with each product, size or weight, retail price and minimum order. Make a separate wholesale list for shops. Always mark prices as current, with a date, because ingredient costs change. For events, offer simple packs, for example a small chops box with two puff-puff and one meat pie, priced per box.
Three selling channels

head: Channel
How to start
Watch out for
rows: Create a business profile, add a catalogue with photos, prices and sizes, post on status at the times people plan orders
Answer quickly, confirm orders in writing, and do not share customers' numbers
Bring a small sample tray and a price list to the bursar, school administrator or office admin; offer a trial week
Agree in writing on quantities, delivery days and payment terms
Show your labelled product and wholesale price list; start with a small quantity
Keep a delivery record signed by the shop; agree whether it is cash, credit or sale-or-return

blocks.title: Worked example: winning a school order
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Owerri wants to supply puff-puff and meat pie to a private secondary school.
steps: She bakes a sample tray of 10 meat pies and 20 puff-puff in clean labelled boxes.
She visits the school administrator with the tray, her price list and photos from her portfolio, and explains her hygiene routine.
The school agrees to a two-week trial: 40 meat pies and 80 puff-puff on Tuesdays and Thursdays, paid every Friday by transfer.
She confirms the agreement in a short WhatsApp message and records every delivery with a signature.
blocks.result: After the trial, the school continues the order. Chioma now has steady weekly volume, which lets her buy flour by the bag and lower her cost per piece.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Fake transfer alerts and fake payment screenshots are common. Never release goods because of an SMS or screenshot alone. Open your own bank, Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay app and confirm the money has arrived in your balance. Never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.
Writing a good catalogue entry

items: **Name and size**: for example, 'Chin chin, 150 g sealed pouch'.
**Price**, marked with the date it was last updated.
**What makes it good**: for example, 'fried fresh every week, no preservatives added' (only if true).
**Allergens**: 'Contains wheat, egg and milk.'
**How to order**: minimum order, delivery areas, and how much notice you need.

blocks.text: Your photos must show the real product at its real size. If a customer receives a meat pie that is smaller than the one in your picture, you lose their trust. Photograph a product from your normal batch next to something familiar, such as a cup, so the size is clear.

If you give shops credit or sale-or-return terms, set a limit. For example, deliver no more than one week's stock on credit, record every delivery and payment, and collect before the next delivery. Unpaid credit is one of the fastest ways a small food business runs out of money.
Collecting payment

Most customers will pay by bank transfer or POS. A business account with a mobile money provider such as Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay, or a business account at your bank, keeps business money separate and gives you a record of every sale. If you take online orders from customers you do not know, payment links from services such as Paystack let you collect payment before you start baking. For big event orders, ask for a deposit, for example 50%, before buying ingredients, and the balance before or on delivery.

Finally, ask happy customers for a short review or a photo you may share, with their permission. A real message from a school or a regular customer is more convincing than anything you can write about yourself.

takeaways: Use clean, food-grade packaging that suits each product and shows it well
Keep dated retail and wholesale price lists, both above your true cost
WhatsApp Business, schools and offices, and shops are three strong channels
Confirm payments in your own banking app; take deposits for large orders

activity.title: Build your sales kit
steps: Set up or update a WhatsApp Business profile with at least three product photos, prices and sizes.
Write a one-page retail price list and a wholesale price list, each dated.
Identify two institutions or shops near you and write down who you will approach.
Visit or message one of them with a sample and your price list, and record the response.
activity.evidence: Screenshot of your WhatsApp Business catalogue, your two price lists, and a note of the outreach response.

lessons.title: Certification checklist and your 90-day growth plan
objectives: Check your portfolio against the certification requirements
Write an honest reflection on what changed after feedback
Set realistic 90-day targets for production and sales
Choose the next skills or courses that will grow your business

blocks.text: You have learned the science, made five products, kept records, costed your work and started selling. This last lesson helps you finish your certificate project honestly and plan the next three months so the progress continues after the course ends.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.alt: A person holding up a certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate rests on real evidence: products, records, costing and feedback.

blocks.text: Certification checklist

blocks.title: Before you submit
items: Two standard recipes in grams
Photos and batch records
Costing sheet with prices
Label draft with allergens
Feedback and reflection
90-day plan
blocks.caption: Tick every item before you attempt the final quiz.

blocks.text: To earn the certificate, you must complete the practical project and score at least **70%** in the final quiz. Submit only your own work. If something did not go well, such as a sunken cake or a batch you had to throw away, include it with what you learned. Honest records of a problem and its fix show more skill than a perfect-looking portfolio with no explanation.

Before you submit, look at your evidence with a customer's eyes. Are the photos dated and clear? Do the weights in your recipes match the weights in your batch records? Does your costing use current prices? Fixing small gaps now makes your portfolio something you can proudly show to a school, a shop or a lender.
Writing your reflection

items: What was your first product like, and what scores did your tasters give?
What one change made the biggest difference, and how do you know?
What does your costing tell you about which product is most profitable?
Which safety habit from the WHO Five Keys did you have to work hardest on?

blocks.text: Preparing for the final quiz

items: The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food and the 5 to 60 C danger zone
What gluten, yeast, baking powder, baking soda, fat and sugar do
Correct oil and oven temperatures for each product
How to scale a recipe with a factor
How to calculate cost per unit and profit margin
What a pre-packaged food label must show, and the basic NAFDAC registration path
How to confirm payments safely

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

A good 90-day plan is short and specific. It names your products, your customers, how often you will produce, and a few numbers to reach. Keep the targets realistic for your time and money. You can always raise them later.

head: Period
Focus
Example target
rows: Steady production of one or two products; fix the weakest quality point
Two production days per week; waste below 10% of units made
Grow one channel: a school, office or shop order
One regular weekly order secured and delivered on time
Strengthen the business: records, separate account, packaging, labels
Monthly profit calculated; business name registered or registration started

blocks.title: Worked example: a 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Bisi from Module 1 now sells puff-puff at the school gate on weekdays and chin chin to neighbours on Saturdays.
steps: Days 1 to 30: she adds a weekly chin chin batch for one shop, and records units sold and waste every week.
Days 31 to 60: she saves part of her profit each week towards a small oven.
Days 61 to 90: she buys the oven, tests meat pie three times with a tasting panel, and adds it to her school offer.
Every Sunday she spends 20 minutes updating her four weekly numbers.
blocks.result: By day 90, Bisi has three products, two steady channels, and records that show her profit each week, which also help if she later applies for a loan or a grant.

blocks.text: A simple weekly tracking sheet

To work out **waste %**, divide the units not sold or rejected by the units made, then multiply by 100. For example, in Week 1 above, 200 made minus 176 sold leaves 24; 24 divided by 200 is 0.12, which is 12%. Falling waste and rising repeat customers are strong signs that your quality and planning are improving.

As you grow, you may bring in a helper. Train them on your written recipes, quality standard and the Five Keys before they handle food, and check their work until you are confident. Your name is on every product, so the standard must stay the same whoever makes it.

blocks.title: Next steps for learning
blocks.text: Good next topics are advanced baking and pastry (bread varieties, decorated cakes), food business record keeping, digital marketing on WhatsApp and Instagram, and business registration. Check the WODDI Institute catalogue for courses that match your plan.

Share your progress with your WODDI learning community. Other women are solving the same problems, from slow-rising dough on cold mornings to finding reliable packaging suppliers. Asking for and giving help is part of building a lasting business.

takeaways: Complete every checklist item and score at least 70% in the final quiz
Include honest records of problems and fixes in your portfolio
A 90-day plan names products, customers, production days and a few numbers
Review your four weekly numbers every week to stay on track

activity.title: Finish and plan
steps: Go through the certification checklist and collect any missing evidence.
Write your reflection using the four questions, in about half a page.
Write your 90-day plan using the three-period table.
Share your plan with one person who will check on your progress at day 30.
activity.evidence: Completed checklist, written reflection and 90-day plan, ready to submit with your portfolio.

quiz.q: Halima must deliver at 10:30 am and the journey takes 30 minutes. Packing and cooling need 1 hour. When must all cooking be finished?
quiz.explain: Work backwards: leave at 10:00 am, so cooling and packing must start by 9:00 am, which means cooking must be finished by 9:00 am.

quiz.q: Which task is safe and sensible to do the day before a meat pie order?
options: Bake the pies and leave them out overnight
Cook the filling, cool it quickly and refrigerate it within 2 hours
Mix puff-puff batter and leave it out overnight
Nothing can be done the day before
quiz.explain: Cooked filling can be chilled safely overnight. Baked pies left out overnight and over-risen batter are risks.

quiz.q: A customer sends a screenshot of a transfer for a big order, but nothing shows in your app yet. What should you do?
options: Release the goods, the screenshot is proof
Wait and confirm the money has arrived in your own account before releasing the goods
Ask for their bank PIN to check
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Only money confirmed in your own account counts.

quiz.q: Chioma wants to supply a school. What is the best first approach?
options: Send a voice note to the principal at midnight
Bring a sample tray, price list and portfolio photos to the administrator and offer a trial
quiz.explain: A sample, clear prices and evidence of hygiene build trust, and a trial lowers the school's risk.

quiz.q: Which 90-day target is the most useful?
options: Become the biggest bakery in Nigeria
Secure one regular weekly order and keep waste below 10% of units made
quiz.explain: Specific, measurable targets let you check progress. Vague goals cannot be measured.

quiz.q: What is the minimum final quiz score for the certificate, alongside the completed practical project?
quiz.explain: Learners qualify after completing the practical project and scoring at least 70% in the final quiz.

finalQuiz.q: Which list correctly states the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food?
options: Keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials
Keep clean; add preservatives; fry everything; refrigerate bread; reuse oil
finalQuiz.explain: These are the five keys WHO uses to teach safe food handling.

finalQuiz.q: Between which temperatures do bacteria multiply fastest?
finalQuiz.explain: 5 to 60 C is the danger zone. Keep perishable food out of it as much as possible.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi's bread dough tears when she stretches it thin. What does this tell her?
options: The dough is ready to bake
The gluten is not yet developed; she should knead longer
finalQuiz.explain: Dough that passes the windowpane test stretches thin without tearing. Tearing means more kneading is needed.

finalQuiz.q: Which ingredient change would make meat pie pastry tough instead of short and flaky?
finalQuiz.explain: Kneading develops gluten, which makes pastry tough. Pastry should be mixed briefly.

finalQuiz.q: What oil temperature range is right for puff-puff?
finalQuiz.explain: At about 170 to 180 C the puff-puff seals and browns while the inside cooks. Cooler oil gives greasy puff-puff.

finalQuiz.q: A pound cake recipe uses 250 g each of fat, sugar, eggs and flour for one tin. How much flour is needed for three tins?
Kemi's cake sank in the middle. She opened the oven door after 10 minutes. What should she change first?
options: Bake at a much higher temperature
Keep the oven door closed for the first half of baking
finalQuiz.explain: Opening the door early lets heat escape before the structure sets. Change this one thing first and test again.

finalQuiz.q: Which item must be on a pre-packaged food label under NAFDAC's 2022 labelling regulations?
finalQuiz.explain: Batch numbers allow each production run to be traced. Health claims must not be made without evidence.

finalQuiz.q: A customer with an egg allergy asks about your chin chin, which contains one egg per batch. What is the right answer?
options: It has only a little egg, so it is fine
Egg is cooked out during frying
There is no egg in fried snacks
finalQuiz.explain: Any amount of egg must be declared. Cooking does not remove allergens.

finalQuiz.q: A meat pie batch costs 7,200 naira in total and gives 24 good pies. What is the cost per pie?
Halima's true cost per pie is 300 naira and she sells at 500 naira. What is her profit margin?
Before releasing a large order paid by transfer, what should a seller always do?
options: Confirm the money has arrived in her own banking or mobile money app
Wait for an SMS alert only
finalQuiz.explain: Fake screenshots and alerts are common. Only money confirmed in her own account is real.

capstone.title: Small chops production order and business portfolio
capstone.brief: Produce a real or practice order of at least 30 pieces using at least two products from the course (one fried, and one baked if you have an oven), and submit a portfolio with standard recipes in grams, production plan, batch records, photos, quality checks, tasting panel scores, a costing sheet with prices, a draft label with allergens, a reflection and a 90-day plan.
steps: Choose two products and write your standard recipes in grams, scaled for the order.
Write a backwards production plan from the delivery time, with a shopping list.
Set up your workstation using the WHO Five Keys and photograph it.
Produce the order, keeping a batch record with weights, temperatures, yield and rejects.
Run the five-point quality check, and have at least three people score the products.
Complete a costing sheet with cost per unit, retail price and wholesale price.
Draft a label for one packaged product with all required elements and allergens.
Write a short reflection on what you changed after feedback, and a 90-day plan.
evidence: Standard recipes in grams with the scaling factor shown
Photos: clean workstation, mise en place, cooking, finished products, cut or broken sample
Completed batch record with batch number
Quality check and tasting panel score sheets
Costing sheet with cost per unit and both prices
Draft label with allergens, net weight, dates and batch number
